analysis.one_liner: Requires 401(k) providers to disclose all fees and gives workers a low-cost index option.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill 29-17, but it sat on a House calendar for more than seven months and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that run 401(k) plans to tell employers and workers up front, in plain dollar terms, every fee being charged — including hidden payments fund companies make to each other and the difference between mutual fund share classes. It would require quarterly statements showing what was deducted from each worker's account, require every plan to offer at least one cheap passively managed index fund, and require that anyone giving workers investment advice be independent rather than selling them the plan's own funds. It would also let employers stretch out pension funding deadlines.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of workers whose retirement savings sit in 401(k) accounts. Hidden fees of even one percent a year can quietly consume a large share of a lifetime of returns; the bill would force those fees into the open in dollar amounts, show them on quarterly statements, and give workers a standard to compare plans against. Workers would also gain access to a low-cost index fund in every plan and to investment advice that does not earn more money by steering them into the adviser's own products.

how_it_helps.text: Service providers would have to give plan administrators a written statement of expected total annual charges, broken into administration, investment management, and transaction fees, before any contract is signed.
Participants would get a plan fee comparison chart listing every charge against their account, plus quarterly statements showing the actual dollar charges deducted each quarter.
Every plan would have to include at least one passively managed index fund covering the U.S. stock or bond market, offered without any endorsement that steers workers toward it.

Investment advice could come only from an independent registered adviser or a certified computer program that cannot favor the adviser's own funds, replacing the existing exemption that let plan providers sell workers self-interested advice.
Service providers that fail to disclose would face civil penalties of up to $1,000 a day, and administrators that fail to give participants the information up to $100 a day.

analysis.who_pays: Mutual fund companies, plan recordkeepers, and brokers who earn the hidden fees — through lost revenue once fees are visible and comparable, plus penalties for nondisclosure. Employers also bear new compliance costs, though small plans get lighter treatment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fund companies, plan service firms, brokers

drawbacks.text: The disclosure rules impose real paperwork and compliance costs on plan administrators and service providers; the bill softens this for small plans by allowing annual instead of quarterly statements for plans with 100 or fewer participants and applying only to service contracts of $5,000 or more a year.

Title III gives employers pension funding relief — stretching amortization periods for single-employer and multiemployer plans and letting sponsors revoke interest-rate elections — which lowers required contributions in the short run at the risk of leaving pensions less well funded.

The bill relies on transparency rather than fee caps; it guarantees that workers can see the charges but not that the charges will come down, since savings depend on employers and workers actually switching to cheaper options.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — fee disclosure in plain dollar terms, quarterly statements showing actual deductions, a mandatory low-cost index option, and independent advice — directly targets a documented cost borne by retirement savers, and the compliance burden is scaled down for small plans. The pension funding relief in Title III is a real trade-off, shifting some near-term contribution pressure onto long-term pension health, but it is a modest sweetener attached to a bill whose main effect is protecting workers' accounts.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared committee with a 29-17 vote, then the House Ways and Means Committee held its share of the bill through eight one-month extensions, and after finally reaching the House calendar in May 2010 no one ever brought it up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California introduced the bill on June 23, 2009, and it was referred to the Education and Labor and Ways and Means Committees.
The Education and Labor Committee ordered it reported as amended by a vote of 29 to 17 the next day, and formally reported it on July 31, 2009.
The House Ways and Means Committee kept its referral alive through eight successive one-month extensions from October 2009 to April 2010 and never marked up the bill.
Ways and Means was finally discharged on May 28, 2010, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, which is the list of bills awaiting a House floor vote.
No floor vote ever occurred before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The mutual fund and retirement-plan service companies that collect the fees the bill would have exposed — and the brokers who could keep selling plan participants self-interested advice — are better off because the bill never became law.

sides.party_line_note: The committee approved the bill 29 to 17, but the record does not break that vote down by party, and the bill's sponsor, cosponsor, and added sponsor were all Democrats.

industries.industry: Mutual fund and investment management firms
industries.note: They would have had to disclose every fee before contracting with plans, reveal how share-class pricing differs inside and outside the plan, and disclose payments from affiliated or third parties. Making these charges visible pressures the asset-based fees that make up most of their 401(k) revenue.
They would face itemized charge disclosure, annual updates, and civil penalties up to $1,000 a day for nondisclosure, plus Labor Department audits of plan compliance.

industries.industry: Brokers and conflicted investment advice providers
industries.note: The bill would strike the existing exemption that let plan providers sell participants advice tied to their own products, allowing only independent registered advisers or certified unbiased computer programs. Workers' gain would come directly out of advice revenue tied to product sales.
The bill creates a legal pathway and a new customer base for fee-only advisers and certified advice programs, who profit only when participants get sound advice.

Title III would let them stretch pension funding over longer periods and revoke interest-rate elections for 2010, easing required contributions after the 2008 crash — relief that helps employers' cash flow but risks leaving pensions less funded over time.
